Anat Cohen

Anat Cohen first played jazz in Tel Aviv, in the Jaffa Conservatory’s Dixieland Band. She has established herself in the U.S. as a respected clarinetist, saxophonist, band leader and performer of jazz and world music.
Anat was interviewed via Zoom on September 9, 2021 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.

My name is Monk Rowe for the Fillius Jazz Archive and Hamilton College Performing Arts, and I’m very pleased to have Anat Cohen with me this morning, not exactly jazz musicians’ hours, but nonetheless I’m pleased to speak with you.
Same here, Monk, very pleased to be speaking with you.

I want to start out with an observation and a comparison. Years ago I was able to interview Buddy DeFranco, the clarinetist, who described the instrument as an “agony stick.” And contrasted with your website where the first thing you see is “the clarinet took over my life and I’m happily surrendering.” So I like that attitude toward your instrument.

Yeah. Well not to disagree with Mr. DeFranco, who I loved very much, it is agony, an agony stick, and it’s an interesting instrument. Sometimes I feel like the more I practice the harder it gets. It’s a bizarre instrument. But when I refer to me surrendering to it I think it’s more, there’s two elements. One is that I was, when I came to the United States from Israel I went to Berklee College of Music as a tenor saxophone player. And I focused on studying jazz as a saxophone player, and the clarinet was always there, I played it before and it accompanied me all through my life, but I didn’t really envision how to become a performer, a soloist on the clarinet in the music that I wanted to do, and it just slowly took over my life, through various music, various — the study of jazz but also study of world music and of being in Boston, a student, and meeting Brazilian people and people from Argentina and then later people from Columbia, and the clarinet started to be, you know, part of different groups and sounds I was playing and of course the music of New Orleans and so suddenly I realized wait a second, I’m playing more clarinet than saxophone. It wasn’t my intention, and I felt I can be who I am, I can be myself on the clarinet. So partially that’s what’s behind the clarinet took over my life and I am happily surrendering because it brought so much joy and so many new encounters and opportunities for me, that I feel very grateful.
In retrospect, has it been perhaps a good decision as far as finding a place in the jazz world, because there’s no lack of tenor saxophone players?

That is correcto. There are definitely no lack of tenor saxophone players, but this, it wasn’t, as I’m saying it wasn’t like oh I want to become a clarinet player because there are plenty of tenor saxophone players. I just found myself in different situations playing clarinet and feeling really comfortable, feeling that — feeling connected to the instrument, something that maybe with a tenor saxophone was not as natural as it was for me on the clarinet. And you know the heavy, the history of jazz and the history of music, really when you think about all the spirit and the fathers of the tenor saxophone, I mean it’s such a heavy, heavy legacy, just being on the stage of the Village Vanguard and feeling like the spirit of Trane there and Joe Henderson, you know the kind of accompaniment that I had was also, you know, something that was with me the whole time. And when I play clarinet somehow, maybe because I started from more of the classical music world, I felt more connection and, oh I’m just going to play the way I play, and it wasn’t as heavy.
If you had stayed in the classical realm in Israel, can you surmise that you might have been able to make a living in that genre? Without coming to America?

I don’t know. I don’t really know. In any kind of music I mean I went to study, I went to college, I went to Berklee College of Music and of course there’s all the curriculum and the academic world and the subjects that I studied, but I think that the main important thing that Berklee gave me is opening the door to the international community and through the people, the other students, expand my horizons and really fall in love with a variety of music that maybe if I stayed in Israel it would have taken me longer to get to. Of course the internet arrived a little later, so it was not like today with the press of a button you’re like, you travel the world. And you look at the world through Google and you can just look at the streets and drive around and listen to music and have radio stations that play music from any era and every point in the world. It wasn’t as easy.

In your bio there’s a brief anecdote about you finally arriving in New York and going to Small’s. And I wonder if that, I can only envision if maybe that was a moment to remember for you — what was that like to sort of step into a club and say okay, this is a big part of the New York scene and how do I fit into this.

Wow that’s a beautiful question because you really brought me back to that moment. I mean the name of the club is called Small’s, which still exists, so I didn’t know what it was. I didn’t know at that time when I stepped into Small’s it was a new club that was encouraging young people to find who they are through the tradition of bebop and hard bop, but open the doors for experiments for people to write their own music and to make their own bands, and I just witnessed a couple of people that I knew, because there was a bass player that I knew since I was in high school, used to play with my older brother Yuval, his name is Omer Avital and Omer was a key figure at the time at Small’s. And I

walked into Small’s and he’s — there he was just playing the bass, swinging his butt off, and being part of the scene. And so for me more than thinking of like what is Small’s or the scenes of New York, for me it was kind of the idea that somebody from Israel, from a different country, from where I come from, from my city, can just be part of a whole new culture and mingle so well and excel. So there was a few other Israelis at the time that were part of that scene, so for me it was, and I remember that night I mean we definitely pulled an all-nighter that trip because we were students, we had no money, we were there at Small’s and we had to spend — Small’s was open the whole night after the shows. There was like a show at 10 PM, at midnight, at 2 AM, then a jam session all night and then of course at 6 AM we took the bus back to Boston where I was still a student at Berklee. So we had to stay there, no matter what, so we were just kind of like watching all these amazing — the hang. The hang basically.
The hang.

It’s the hang, which is part of what we do, right? It’s like I always say this anecdote, there was this teacher at Berklee, a guy who was always busy and like running — no I’ve got to go do homework, I’ve got to go do this, I’ve got to go — and then the teacher told me, “Anat, you’ve got to learn how to hang.” And I’m like okay. So — a work in progress.
Yeah.
It’s good. I like the hang.
Did the hang translate, help translate into your stage presence, which I observe as welcoming and an addition to what you can present?

You know it’s interesting, I mean first of all I’m glad you feel it’s welcoming and you know I don’t know if it’s the hang — I think part of what made me feel comfortable on stage was being part of an Afro-Cuban band — it’s a band in Boston called, it used to be called Mango Blue, then it became Mango Blues, and I was in the saxophone section with Miguel Zenon, the great alto player. And I didn’t know much about Afro-Cuban music or all the South American rhythm, it was all new to me, but another thing that was definitely new to me is dancing. And being on stage, playing, you know, sometimes there would be a long piano solo and everybody, basically looking at the audience everybody is dancing, and I’m realizing okay I cannot just be on stage standing still. It’s not part of the culture, it’s not part of the music, so I was very embarrassed at the beginning and then I’m like okay I can just move and then slowly I got more relaxed into it, and then when there’d be long solos I would just leave my saxophone on stage and go in the audience and just start dancing with people and dance with Miguel on the stage looking, learning the steps. And I think after being able to not worry about what other people think because I’m dancing, it’s just a whole other cultural aspect that is not — I didn’t learn in Israel. I think after that, being on stage and just playing and concentrating on the music and
moving to the moment and being in the moment I don’t think about the stage as a stage. I just think it’s like let’s just all celebrate the moment.
Beautiful. I want to ask you about two specific performances that are viewable for people, one is the “Tiny Desk” concert you did, Marcello Goncalves — is that correct?
Um hum. Yes.

And it’s really interesting to watch. First of all there’s no music in front of you and this one particular song, I’m not sure you opened your eyes at all. So this could be a — may not even have an answer, but can you describe what’s going on in your head in a kind of performance like that? Is some of it, okay here comes that chord that I have to remember to observe in my playing? Or is it different than that?

Wow that’s a really — it’s an interesting question because there’s no absolute answer to that. The goal is not to have those thoughts that you just described, because we spend hours and hours on our craft so once we get to the moment of truth, which means being on stage or being filmed, you can surrender a hundred percent to the music and be in the moment, and really be in tune with that bigger thing, which is the music, which is beyond what I know and what I can do and what I need — it’s what the music needs, and how to connect with the other person and how to connect with the rest of the world. And I think that’s the goal. I think if you are, and that kind of takes me to think about improvisation and playing jazz, if you are playing a song and concentrating on oh that moment is coming and I need to think about the chord — if you’re thinking about what is upcoming and making a plan you are no longer in the moment so you’re losing the moment. So of course it’s kind of incredible I think, you know and you mentioned the classical world and the classical music and the high skill it takes for a musician to execute what they need to do on their instrument, on the whole craft of playing an instrument, being an instrumentalist and being an improviser and being a connector and a communicator, it’s a lot of things and we have a lot of thoughts. In other moments I will be on stage and maybe I’ll start thinking about, wait did I shut off the gas before I left the house or did I — or you know, or somebody would walk into the club and you’re like oh wow wait, I forgot to call or they e-mailed me. Who knows? So many different thoughts can come in into while you’re playing a solo, and it’s like you know when we’re meditating and we have thoughts. And do we surrender to them and let them take over or just like okay shew — it’s a thought, concentrate, go back, distraction. But I think the goal is to get to that connection with the moment that’s really, those tiny moments where you are — it’s the safest place in the world I think when you’re inside the music sphere, when you are connected with the music, with the other musicians, everybody is like in that place and you are laser focused on the moment. And there is some kind of like, you feel the energy of the audience and you feel the energy of — everything just clicks and comes together

and makes sense. And sometimes it’s the most obvious thing. It makes sense. Music can be something so simple and those are like tiny, tiny moments in a whole many many hours of like confusion and frustration and battles and travels. So this is the goal is to get to those moments, to work on our craft to a point where we could master those moments and really bring them to life.
Do you choose your band members and accompanists with that in mind? Like these particular players are most likely to help me get to those moments of truth?

Yes and no. The thought is not they’re going to help me get to the moment of truth, it’s more of like there are people that, with a sense of exploration with a level of listening and respect, and a lever of creativity that is going to challenge but not over bury. So it’s like the musicians that I choose, okay, I like flexible musicians that can go with the moment and not say oh I only know one thing so that’s what I’m going to play.
What would you do if you played something during an improvised solo that you didn’t like?

I’ll tell you what I do, I laugh. You would watch me often, I laugh at myself loudly in front of everybody. I don’t care. I mean because the experiment is I want to try and I’m like, wow that was a bad idea I don’t know what you were thinking. No. That ain’t gonna happen, that did not work. So sometimes it makes me laugh with like the chutzpah that I have to try something like that.

Would your, I assume you had a classical clarinet teacher early on, and I wonder if they saw you playing on a video, I noticed the one thing I was going to ask you about next, a video with Paquito D’Rivera, and at one point you took, I guess it was your left hand and you put it down at your side while you were playing. Now, and also during this particular solo, you used some lovely vibrato. So I’m wondering if your classical teacher might have looked at that and go oh Anat, you shouldn’t be doing that?

Well my classical teacher, I had one main teacher when I was, before I transformed into jazz life, when I was studying a little bit of classical clarinet and her name is Eva Wasserman, she still lives in Israel. And she has been very supportive of my path and she calls me up and she’s proud of me, and she saw me early on moving away from that strict, strictly classical world and she supported it. And she never made a comment that something is wrong. But it’s always interesting, you know I think years of playing saxophone invaded into my clarinet playing. So what I allowed myself to study and to practice on the saxophone I allow myself to do on the clarinet. So maybe it’s not strictly a clarinet approach and not something that a clarinet teacher might teach you, but that’s something that Illinois Jacquet inspired me to play on the tenor saxophone and I’m like okay, I just happened to hold a different horn but the music is, it’s not about the instrument it’s about what’s inside.
That particular moment with the vibrato for some reason made me think of Kenny Davern. You had that particular tone and he’s been a favorite of mine and so I now have another favorite with you.

I loved Kenny Davern you know. It’s kind of — he was important in my path. Because years ago I played with, I played for many years with the Diva Jazz Orchestra, an all- female big band that exists for over 25 years. And we played the Clearwater Jazz Festival, it was around the year 2000. And it was Flip Phillips’ 85th birthday and at the end of the festival in the hotel everybody played “Happy Birthday” to Flip Phillips on stage, a bunch of musicians, including Buddy DeFranco and Kenny Davern. And Stanley Kay, the manager of Diva asked me, “Where is your clarinet?” And I’m like, “It’s in the hotel room.” It didn’t even occur to me, I wasn’t even, I was still playing saxophone. He says, “Go get it.” So I went to my room and by the time I came back to the stage they were already playing rhythm changes and you know everybody took a couple of choruses and I just went on stage and I went to the clarinet and I went to the front and I played two choruses of rhythm changes and then the minute I finished I had two hands grab me by the shoulder and led me back and it was Kenny Davern who held me and took me back and put me right between him and Buddy DeFranco. And that was a really, really important moment for me because it was a moment of his saying all right girl, you’re with us, which was — it still took me a minute to become a clarinetist but it was a really memorable moment, important.

Thanks for sharing that. I love that story. And speaking of important people the tune with Paquito D’Rivera was called “And the World Weeps.” And I’ve been in a situation a couple of times in my life where I was playing next to someone I really admired or was a mentor or teacher. And I was wondering if you were thinking, because he soloed first, and beautifully, did you allow yourself to have these kind of somewhat negative thoughts like what am I going to do now? You know I would have done what he did but he already did it. Or it sounds like maybe you don’t let those kind of things get into your head.

I just, you know I just have a different approach because what would I do now, for me, is a positive thought, not a negative thought. Because if he played something and he left me to a point, say a challenge, what do I have to add? How can I add to the music after everything that he already gave? So for me it’s not like oh my God he played so beautiful now I’m going to — I mean there’s no time and no room for negative thoughts at this point, it’s only about think about the music and you have to really be — sometimes go into something that maybe you haven’t tried yet. Maybe I haven’t played before but the moment wants something else. So that’s what I’m saying if I was planning what I’m going to play and then Paquito has played it I would be like — not be in the moment and not be able to add anything because I would be all confused. So you know, but Paquito is

definitely somebody I admire so much and it was such a thrill to have him, it was the D.C. Jazz Festival and actually he recorded that tune with me on my album Ciaroscuro, that “And the World Weeps.” It’s a Dr. Lonnie Smith song, a very simple minor eight bars, the song is just powerful and simple like many songs. And it’s just great because it can really show how for me how to be connected with your soul and how the clarinet can be so expressive and get such a wide range of emotions. And Pacquito is such an inspiration, the way he plays the clarinet, his sound on the clarinet, the kind of genres and music he dives into and what he presents in one show. And for somebody that was, you know I moved to New York and I was all confused about, oh I want to do this music or that music, how do you play — he’s a person that combines his classical roots with his love for Brazilian music with his Cuban roots to love of Argentinean music, for the world traveler, and he makes it be one thing and it was very inspiring for me to say hold on, I connect all of those things. It’s not — the music might be different from different places but the way we’re going to be playing it with the band we’re going to make it ours. So he was inspiring.

You’ve done very well in the polls, DownBeat, in the last few years, and I wonder if people who are voting for you, if it’s more than the way — how am I — I’m trying to say that people will like what you do not just because of the way you play your instrument, it’s the music you choose to play, at least this is my attitude. Do you think part of your success in those pollings have to do with what you’ve done with combining music and the variety of things you present?

I don’t know. I don’t know, the mystery of the clarinet, and I talked about it at the beginning of our conversation, the certain natural connection. And at the time I remember my first shows as a band leader I played tenor saxophone for the whole show and I played one song on the clarinet, because at the beginning I was, as I mentioned, the clarinet took over my life, right? I was playing saxophone and clarinet was there waiting, lurking, in the corner. So I would play one song on the clarinet in the whole show and then people would come to talk to me after the show and they would just talk about the clarinet. And I was like okay, but also saying okay maybe the way I play it, I don’t know, it reaches them. I don’t know. I don’t have a reason. I don’t think I’m a better clarinetist than so many others, and everybody has something to offer. So this is all one big mystery for me. But I’m grateful for people to, first of all to accepting the clarinet as an instrument they are willing to listen to and to like, which is already a big step. So many people have preconceptions about the clarinet and they associate it — you know you say jazz and clarinet and people still say, “Ah, Benny Goodman.” And I’m like okay yes, Benny Goodman but there’s more to it than this. So that’s all I am trying to do.
Was there a point — you do some composing and did the clarinet start becoming the instrument you were hearing in your head instead of the saxophone if you were working on a musical idea?

You know it’s a good question because I rarely compose on the clarinet or on the instrument. I compose a melody like that I hear or something that I end up playing on the keyboards or the piano or on the Rhodes and then I figure out which instrument will give it the best character. So the melody is almost inseparable. But one of the — I have one composition that I know for sure I wrote playing the clarinet which is one of my songs called Waltz of the South, “Valsa de Sul.” And that song is very clarinetistic — clarintistic I guess, it uses all the range of the instrument and it would be hard to play it on the soprano saxophone. So maybe I should try and do that more. Yeah, I will.

Start from the clarinet, yeah. You know that’s right, you performed that tune with Marcello I think, yes, and I know what you’re saying. Like I couldn’t reproduce this on another instrument. That’s what’s so nice about the clarinet that the low range is friendly not so much like on the tenor saxophone trying to play way down at the bottom of the horn expressively, I’ve never mastered that for sure.

It’s a challenging one. It’s possible to master and it has a whole other softness when you play those subtones on the tenor saxophone, it gives a whole other feeling to it. But yeah, they’re very different character and each instrument I play I bring a little side of my personality out. I don’t know if I can be everything on — nobody can be everything they are in every given moment.

Historically, in the history of jazz it’s been a male dominated business, getting better. I wonder if you feel like you’ve been at a disadvantage or an advantage as being a woman jazz musician or if it just doesn’t matter anymore?

I don’t know the answer. And I can’t tell. Especially this day and age with the Me Too movement. I don’t think I will know if people hire me to play in a festival because I fill in the quota of they have to have women or because they like the music I play. And I will never know what was the reason before. But when people close their eyes and they don’t know who’s playing, the music has no gender and no color and no flag. Music is just music. So I don’t have an answer for that.
Well you’re very quotable I must say that.
I’m very quotable.
You’re very quotable.
All right.

I would imagine like all other musicians and most people, you had a challenge during this Covid pandemic as far as gigs. Did you stay in the States or did you go home, or do you still think of Israel as home?

Yeah, Israel will always be home, there’s where I grew up, that’s where my mom and my siblings are, and I love it. I just spent one month there and it was incredible. I love Tel Aviv, my city. I love driving around on my scooter and I love being able to stop and go into the city, the city is right on the beach and it’s a lovely city. Complex place but a lovely, lovely city. But when the pandemic started I went down to Rio De Janeiro, and I thought it was just for a little bit. And I stayed there for a while. So the “Tiny Desk” concert you saw was filmed in Rio De Janeiro, it was filmed during the pandemic.

I’m remembering the thing you said about the Latin band in Boston and that you learned to move to the music and it gave me this flash like when I’ve tried to listen to Latin music sometimes I get aggravated, like I lose “one.” And I’m wondering if moving like that helps like keep one in your head.

You know that’s always, what you’re describing is always that conflict between the feeling and the thinking. Because what you feel is what you feel and nobody can argue with you. It’s always right, that’s what you feel. Now whether one person calls it “one” and another person calls it “four” that’s a whole other question and that’s when you want to write music or analyze music then maybe you need to know where is “one.” But the feeling is the feeling so there is first that. But it was not a natural thing for me to find “one” when there’s a clave and to be able to like [snaps fingers] to think and when the clave is moving and to talk about it and I was like okay where is the one, how do you know which one is the clave. Like it took me a while, and through dancing it definitely helped me stable that confidence. And you know my friend Jovino Santos Neto he is a great musician, he played for years with Hermeto Pascoal, a great educator and musician. He’s a piano player. And he talks about, you know, to incorporate a rhythm and the word “corpo” incorpo, the word “body” is in to incorporate. So you’ve got to move. You’ve got to dance, you’ve got to feel it with your body. And I think for me at different kinds of South American rhythms that I encountered, moving, dancing, stepping with the feet and first trusting the body movement, and then thinking about how it feels but going with the feeling first, it helped me understand a lot of music, and hanging out. Hang. Hanging out with the locals.

Do you have hopes for what your audience is absorbing from your music? There’s things that happen onstage that you and musicians in general think oh that was a wonderful moment. Or if you write a melody, I’m trying to form this question about what do you think your audience is hearing in contrast to what you’re hearing?

I would love to interview the audience. I don’t know in contrast to what I’m hearing. I don’t know what — I don’t know how they perceive the music but I know that ultimately the notes, they’re just a tool you know, the goal is to create an emotional impact, to let people — I can’t say forget about their lives for a moment because you know music like

scent, like smell, it brings you back to moments in your life easily. Like you will hear a song that you heard when you were a kid and you’re like oh my God, I just remembered this moment. Or you smell something from the garden of your neighbors that you’re like I know this smell and it brings you back to a moment. So I don’t know if music can always let people forget about their lives or remind them of things they try to forget or wanted to remember, but I do want my music to have an emotional impact and I want it to be meaningful. Also for me. I mean I’m a little bit selfish here, because you know I don’t want to go to the other side of the world and you know, do three Covid tests and travel and you know go take a few flights and then to arrive to a place and just play notes. That’s not enough for me. I want to get off stage and to know that it was meaningful to me, that I connected with the other musicians and by that hoping to be connected to the audience and to take them with me on a little journey, away from their moment. So that’s all.
Okay. Do you have someone who has given you career advice over the years?

Wow. There’s little mentors, there’s little phrases here and there, but you know there’s career and then there’s music and there’s a lot of elements to my journey. But a person that has been extremely helpful and by my side as far as suggestions and support and running our record label is Oded Lev-Ari. Oded is my high school friend and he is the musical director of the tentet, the project that we have together, and he’s also the person that really runs Anzic Records because all the albums that I recorded came out on our own label, a label we established together in 2007, 5, 7. And so, and he is a brilliant musician, a brilliant man, brilliant at so many things, and has a vision for, you know, supports me, knows me, and tells me the truth and by my side in my releases and business advice but also ideas. It’s good to have somebody like that in my life. I think I would really be lost without him. And of course, okay sure, let’s talk about Oded and then we’ll talk about my brothers.
Okay. I just was curious if he composed this song “Putty Boy Strut”?

No the song “Putty Boy Strut” was composed by Flying Lotus, also known as Steve Allison. But Oded composed a concerto for the tentet and myself that we premiered in Carnegie Hall a couple of years ago and it’s the title album “Triple Helix” is the name of the concerto, it’s also the title album of the last tentet album that was nominated for a Grammy for best large ensemble. Exciting.
Well you were mentioning your brothers. And I wonder how your parents have felt about three of their children in the world of jazz?

I don’t know they probably never thought they would retire. It was like what were you thinking? How did you let the three of us become jazz musicians? They, first of all the parents, I wish everybody had supportive parents like that, that see that their children,

they like something, they are into it and they are dedicated to it and they’re like okay we step out of the way, even if we have worries about how you’re going to survive and what’s going to happen, we’re going to let you do what you’re want to do and support you and help you pay for music lessons and drive you around and drive you around and drive you around, and go to all your youth orchestra concerts and, you know they were there when we were squeaking and they were there when The Three Cohens, with the three of us have a sextet and Avishai my younger brother the trumpet player, and Yuval, my older brother, the saxophone player, we have a sextet and when The Three Cohens Sextet played Carnegie Hall my mother was sitting in the audience and you know, and we introduced her and she got up and she was like doing the royal wave to everybody. So that’s the payment they get.

Oh that’s a happy story. Well I appreciate you taking the time to speak with me and I’m looking forward to hearing you live. When you get to a particular venue that you haven’t been to before does the sort of physical layout, the stage, the auditorium affect your choice of repertoire?

It might not affect the choice of repertoire, it depends of course. It depends if it’s a band that has played enough that we have flexibility with repertoire, it might affect. But it definitely affects the way we play. It’s the whole, it’s the type of reverb in the room, it’s the type of instruments that are provided. I bring my own clarinet but the piano player, in this case when we’re going to be playing tomorrow at Hamilton College, there, we’re playing with a new band called Quartetinho and Quartetinho it’s a part of the tentet. So we have Vitor Goncalves playing piano. Of course piano players are always depending on what kind of instrument their hands lay on, and then the vibraphone player and percussion player, James Shipp, I mean he plays the vibraphone, each vibraphone has a different sound, the motor works differently. So it affects, ultimately it also affects the music and the way things resonate and the way we can play with the natural reverb of the instrument, and of course not to mention bass players that a long time ago already had to figure out whatever they like, it’s a Russian roulette. Okay? It’s up and down. So there is that. So it does, everything makes a difference but we try to make the best of every moment.
All right.

And there’s a new album coming out. We’re going to be recording with Quartetinho with a small band at the end of this month. I know we’re in September 2021 now but we’ll be recording so it will come out next year. But also next month I have a new album coming out with Marcello Goncalves. So that’s what happens when you spend the pandemic, you have time to work on music and record and it’s a reflection of the year of work and the
album is called “Reconvexo” which is a song by Caetano Veloso and it has a lot of singer-songwriter songs from Brazil. So I’m excited about that.
Well I’m definitely looking forward to meeting you personally and hearing your music tomorrow.
Yay, me too.
Best of luck with the rest of your career. How’s that for a long term investment?

Yeah. It’s kind of interesting because after being home for a year and a half it kind of went for a second here from zero to a hundred. And it’s a little bit overwhelming I have to say, but you know I’m also very grateful and enjoy it while it lasts because we don’t know what’s going to happen tomorrow. So there’s opportunity to play a few shows and to play live for people and I’m really really excited about that, because I did miss the exchange with the audience, to feel other people, to share energy, so I’m very excited and happy and grateful to be able to have this opportunity tomorrow and in general.
All right. Thanks again.
Thank you, Monk.
Bye-bye.
Bye.

segments.title: Opening, copyright and introductions
segments.summary: Copyright notice, biographical note and Monk Rowe's greeting to Anat Cohen on Zoom.

segments.title: The clarinet took over my life: from tenor at Berklee to clarinet
segments.summary: Cohen agrees the clarinet is an agony stick, and explains how the study of world music in Boston slowly made her a clarinetist.

segments.title: Tenor saxophone legacy versus the clarinet's lighter feel
segments.summary: She says she did not choose clarinet for market reasons; the tenor's heavy legacy felt weightier than clarinet.

segments.title: What Berklee gave her beyond the classical path in Israel
segments.summary: Asked about a classical career in Israel, she says Berklee opened her to an international community and varied music.

segments.title: First night at Small's and seeing Omer Avital
segments.summary: Her first visit to Small's in New York, seeing Omer Avital play, and an all-night hang before the bus back to Boston.

segments.title: Learning to hang, advice from a Berklee teacher
segments.summary: A Berklee teacher told her she had to learn how to hang; she still calls it a work in progress.

segments.title: Mango Blue Afro-Cuban band and learning to dance on stage
segments.summary: Playing in a Boston Afro-Cuban band beside Miguel Zenon taught her to dance and be relaxed on stage.

segments.title: Mind during performance: the Tiny Desk concert and being in the moment
segments.summary: She describes surrendering to the music, avoiding planning ahead, and the rare moments when everything clicks.

segments.title: Choosing bandmates and laughing at failed ideas
segments.summary: She picks flexible, listening musicians, and laughs at herself when an improvised idea fails.

segments.title: Classical teacher Eva Wasserman and saxophone ideas on clarinet
segments.summary: Her classical teacher supported her move to jazz; her sax studies and Illinois Jacquet shaped her clarinet playing.

segments.title: Kenny Davern pulls her on stage at the Clearwater festival
segments.summary: Playing with Diva Jazz Orchestra, she was told to fetch her clarinet and Kenny Davern placed her between himself and Buddy DeFranco.

segments.title: Playing after Paquito D'Rivera and recording 'And the World Weeps'
segments.summary: She treats following Paquito as a positive challenge, and describes his recording on Claroscuro and his inspiration to her.

segments.title: DownBeat polls and the mystery of the clarinet's appeal
segments.summary: She cannot explain her poll success, recalls playing one clarinet tune per show, and notes the Benny Goodman stereotype.

segments.title: Composing away from the clarinet, and the tenor's subtones
segments.summary: She composes on keyboards, except 'Valsa de Sul' written on clarinet; each instrument brings out a side of her.

segments.title: Being a woman in jazz: music has no gender
segments.summary: She cannot know whether she is hired for quotas or music, and says music has no gender, color or flag.

segments.title: Israel as home and the pandemic spent in Rio
segments.summary: Israel is home; she describes Tel Aviv and says the Tiny Desk concert was filmed in Rio during the pandemic.

segments.title: Finding 'one' in Latin rhythms through dancing
segments.summary: Feeling comes before thinking; dancing helped with clave, and Jovino Santos Neto speaks of incorporating rhythm in the body.

segments.title: What she hopes audiences hear: emotional impact and meaning
segments.summary: Notes are a tool; she wants music to have emotional impact and be meaningful to her and the audience.

segments.title: Oded Lev-Ari, Anzic Records and the tentet
segments.summary: Her high school friend Oded runs Anzic Records, directs the tentet and wrote the Triple Helix concerto; Putty Boy Strut is Flying Lotus's.

segments.title: Her parents and the Three Cohens at Carnegie Hall
segments.summary: Supportive parents of three jazz musicians; their mother waved at the Three Cohens sextet's Carnegie Hall show.

segments.title: How venue layout and instruments affect the performance
segments.summary: Room reverb, pianos and vibraphones change how Quartetinho plays, with a show at Hamilton College next day.

segments.title: New albums: Quartetinho and Reconvexo with Marcello Goncalves
segments.summary: She is recording with Quartetinho and has an album of Brazilian songs, Reconvexo, coming next month.

segments.title: Closing: returning to live performance
segments.summary: Thanks and goodbyes; she is excited and overwhelmed to be playing for audiences again after the pandemic.
